stem:
In the following table, every entry on the left column can match with any number of entries on the right side. Pick up **all** those and write respectively against A, B, C and D.

| Name of the force | | Type of the force | |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Force due to tension in a string | P | EM force |
| B | Normal force | Q | Reaction force |
| C | Frictional force | R | Conservative force |
| D | Resistive force offered by air or water for objects moving through it. | S | Non-conservative force |
In real life objects, never travel with uniform velocity, even on a horizontal surface, unless something is done? Why is it so? What is to be done?
_note: Printed as shown. The book's punctuation is defective twice in one sentence: the comma belongs after "In real life" (it is printed after "objects"), and the sentence is declarative yet terminated with a question mark. Transcribed verbatim; not repaired.

stem: For the study of any kind of motion, we never use Newton's first law of motion directly. Why should it be studied?

subtopic: Inertial and Non-Inertial Frames of Reference
stem: Are there any situations in which we cannot apply Newton's laws of motion? Is there any alternative for it?

subtopic: Inertial and Non-Inertial Frames of Reference
stem: You are inside a closed capsule from where you are not able to see anything about the outside world. Suddenly you feel that you are pushed towards your right. Can you explain the possible cause (s)? Is it a feeling or a reality? Give at least one more situation like this.
Among the four fundamental forces, only one force governs your daily life almost entirely. Justify the statement by stating that force.
Find the odd man out: (i) Force responsible for a string to become taut on stretching (ii) Weight of an object (iii) The force due to which we can hold an object in hand.

You are sitting next to your friend on ground. Is there any gravitational force of attraction between you two? If so, why are you not coming together naturally? Is any force other than the gravitational force of the earth coming in picture?
Distinguish between: (A) Real and pseudo forces, (B) Conservative and non-conservative forces, (C) Contact and non-contact forces, (C) Inertial and non-inertial frames of reference.
_note: Printed as shown. The book labels FOUR sub-parts (A), (B), (C), (C) - the letter (C) is repeated and the fourth item should be labelled (D). Verified at 3x zoom on p-28 (both glyphs are an open C, distinct from the closed-loop D used elsewhere on the page). Transcribed verbatim; not repaired.

stem: State the formula for calculating work done by a force. Are there any conditions or limitations in using it directly? If so, state those clearly. Is there any mathematical way out for it? Explain.
Justify the statement, "Work and energy are the two sides of a coin".

From the terrace of a building of height \(H\), you dropped a ball of mass \(m\). It reached the ground with speed \(v\). Is the relation \(mgH = \frac{1}{2} m v^2\) applicable exactly? If not, how can you account for the difference? Will the ball bounce to the same height from where it was dropped?

subtopic: Principle of Conservation of Linear Momentum
stem: State the law of conservation of linear momentum. It is a consequence of which law? Given an example from our daily life for conservation of momentum. Does it hold good during burst of a cracker?
_note: Printed as shown. The book prints "Given an example" where the imperative "Give an example" is intended. Transcribed verbatim; not repaired.

stem: Define coefficient of restitution and obtain its value for an elastic collision and a perfectly inelastic collision.

Discuss the following as special cases of elastic collisions and obtain their exact or approximate final velocities in terms of their initial velocities.
(i) Colliding bodies are identical.
(ii) A veru heavy object collides on a lighter object, initially at rest.
(iii) A very light object collides on a comparatively much massive object, initially at rest.
_note: Printed as shown. Sub-item (ii) prints "A veru heavy object" - a typo for "very". Verified at 3x zoom on p-28; sub-item (iii) on the very next line spells "very" correctly, which is what identifies (ii) as a misprint. Transcribed verbatim; not repaired.

stem: A bullet of mass \(m_1\) travelling with a velocity \(u\) strikes a stationary wooden block of mass \(m_2\) and gets embedded into it. Determine the expression for loss in the kinetic energy of the system. Is this violating the principle of conservation of energy? If not, how can you account for this loss?
One of the effects of a force is to change the momentum. Define the quantity related to this and explain it for a variable force. Usually when do we define it instead of using the force?

subtopic: Moment of a Force and Torque
stem: While rotating an object or while opening a door or a water tap we apply a force or forces. Under which conditions is this process easy for us? Why? Define the vector quantity concerned. How does it differ for a single force and for two opposite forces with different lines of action?
Why is the moment of a couple independent of the axis of rotation even if the axis is fixed?
Explain balancing or mechanical equilibrium. Linear velocity of a rotating fan as a whole is generally zero. Is it in mechanical equilibrium? Justify your answer.
Why do we need to know the centre of mass of an object? For which objects, its position may differ from that of the centre of gravity?
